                                         We introduce Hierarchical Streaming Video Understanding,
                                         a task that combines online temporal action localization
                                         with free-form description generation. Given the scarcity                                                                                          Time(s)

                                         erarchical Online Understanding System for Events), which
                                         extends streaming action perception beyond action classifi-                          Changing the wheel                Repairing the brake

                                         cation. OpenHOUSE features a specialized streaming mod-

                                                                                                             task into two parts: (i) a lightweight “streaming” perception
                                            This highlights the need for an instantaneous, open-
                                                                                                             module that processes each frame and performs hierarchy-
                                         ended and hierarchical understanding of streaming input
                                                                                                             aware action detection in real time, calling the VLM only
                                         (Figure 1). Large-scale Vision Language Models (VLMs)
                                                                                                             when needed, and (ii) a VLM that generates descriptions
                                         [1, 30, 31], with their powerful reasoning capabilities, are
                                                                                                             only when called by the perception module. This disen-
                                         well-suited for handling this challenge. However, apply-
                                                                                                             tanglement offers distinct advantages over a single model
                                         ing VLMs to continuous visual streams presents unique
                                                                                                             approach. First, it enables efficient operation by continu-

Figure 4. (a) Illustration of OpenHOUSE. The lightweight Streaming module processes every frame, while VLM inference is triggered
selectively at T = 3, 4, 8, 10, indicated by the yellow bell icon. (b) Diagram depicting how our hybrid action boundary detection works.
For instance, at T 2, a sudden drop in the progression signals the action end, marking the current frame as a background frame. In the next
timestep, a high actionness score (= 1.0) classifies the frame as an action frame, resulting in a background-to-action transition and marking
it as the start of Ins2.

Ideally, both action ends and starts should be marked as                 For example, assume that the Streaming module detects

Hybrid action boundary detection To address this issue,              instead of using uniform sampling, which could overlook
we introduce a novel strategy for determining action bound-          important details. This, along with a customized prompt
aries. In addition to measuring actionness, we also measure          for the step hierarchy, is passed to the VLM, producing ap-
the “progress” of action instances and detect sudden drops           propriate description. The prediction is then added to the
in this progress to signify action ends. Note that ground-           context memory for future use. Exact prompts and other

and “Exo.” denotes EgEx’s Exo view. “GT proposal” refers to experiments using ground truth action proposals as VLM input, without class
information. Zero-shot VLM inference achieves around 30% accuracy in matching ground truth labels. InternVL2-40B-AWQ [6] is used
as the frozen VLM. Following the original implementation, YT-Temporal [50] pretrained Vid2Seq [48] weights are used for initialization
of SDVC, and fine-tuned using EgoGS annotations, with separate training for each hierarchy. We used the default configuration on SDVC.

Figure 6. (a) tIoU -based Hungarian matching. Hungarian matching provides optimal one-to-one matching in terms of maximizing
tIoU, unlike greedy matching which allows duplication. Here, the algorithm selects ”Rinse vegetables” as the best match for the GT
”Wash vegetables”. With a predefined tIoU threshold of 0.3, ”Rinse vegetables” is considered a True Positive (TP), while the unmatched
prediction ”Turn on faucet” is classified as a False Positive (FP). If no prediction matches the GT or fails to meet the threshold, the
instance is counted as a False Negative (FN). (b) The description ”Rinse vegetables”, initially marked as a TP in F1 (loc.), is encoded into
an embedding vector. Similarly, all GT descriptions in the test split are encoded, and pairwise cosine similarities are computed. If ”Wash
vegetables” appears among the top 5 most similar GT descriptions, ”Rinse vegetables” is confirmed as a TP.

Figure 7. An example of calculating GPT, or BERTscore. With a tIoU threshold of 0.3, the predictions ”Turn on faucet” and ”Rinse
vegetables” are matched with the GT ”Wash vegetables”, while ”Hold knife” is matched with ”Grip knife”. This duplicated matching
with ”Wash vegetables” highlights a key difference from the Hungarian F1 metric. After matching, GPT-Score or BERTscore is computed
for each matched pair, and the final score is obtained by averaging all pair scores.
